_comment: C0-5 body translation for coding/meta-muse. Keys align with build.mjs: axes by axis key; sections/sectionTitles by the Chinese headings of extraSections (10 sections); runs/unknowns/related/sources by index alignment.
_rules: 0) Keep ** emphasis, `code`, links and table structure, block-for-block with the Chinese side.
1) Official English quotes stay verbatim; Chinese-rendered paraphrases of official wording are marked (translated) on the English side — never fabricate English originals.
2) Do not upgrade 'unverified / not stated officially' semantics; the translation changes no facts.

axes.model_access:
**The model is vendor-assigned** — **official wording**: "powered by Muse Spark, Meta's most capable model to date, built for real-world agentic work like this".

Muse Spark is a separate Meta model name (the Meta Careers page lists **official wording**: "Muse Spark · natively multimodal reasoning, visual chain of thought and multi-agent orchestration" as its own entry).

**There is no model-selection entry point.** The same model name also appears in AI-glasses release notes (Muse Spark on Meta Ray-Ban Display) — it is reused across form factors.
axes.runtime:
**The answer to "what form is it" is the product itself**: the official wording says Muse runs on a **Muse Secure VM**,
described officially as **official wording**: "a dedicated, virtual machine (VM) that houses both the agent and a person's data", and **official wording**: "Every Muse user's VM is isolated so no one else's agent can access it" (see the Help Centre page).

**The entry-point story differs from local agents**: the official pages stress **official wording**: "talking to it works just like messaging another person, in the Muse app or directly in WhatsApp" —
**WhatsApp is one of the entry points**, a clear difference from the other two vendors.

Launch channels: iOS / Android / muse.ai, US first, officially **official wording**: "coming soon to AI glasses".
axes.local_files:
**It is not designed to read or write files on your machine**; the official text never mentions the local file system.

All data lives in the Muse Secure VM.

The official pages add a data-minimization promise for app connections (Help Centre page):
**"For example, connecting your email allows Muse to search your email"** **"but it won't download your whole inbox (unless you tell it to)"**.

**This sentence is a concrete boundary the official pages give on the data side, worth noting separately.**
axes.background:
**The official pages state the after-close behavior explicitly**, more concrete than just "always on":
**official wording**: "For tasks that take more time, Muse keeps working after people close the app, and comes back when something changes or when it needs approval, like before it sends an email or makes a purchase".

i.e. **continuous background work + callbacks only for approvals**.

**The "come back" triggers are listed officially in three classes** (Help Centre approval page):

- Task progress (status bar shows "Is working" / "Making something" / "Is updating memory" live)
- Scheduled tasks or reminders coming due (inside the assistant icon, **Upcoming** lists scheduled tasks and reminders, and each scheduled task can have its own approval setting)
- And the moment your approval is needed

One official sentence uses "proactively":
**official wording**: "a personal AI agent that proactively helps with people's goals and suggests ideas"
and it can **official wording**: "make suggestions unprompted".

**The trigger source is not only your commands** — the Help Centre Connector page describes reverse pushes:
**official wording**: "Some Connectors can also share information proactively with Muse. For example, calendar Connectors can update Muse automatically when there are changes in your schedule", and **such Connectors are flagged before connection**.

**Read-only or read-write during autonomous background work? This entry gives a mechanism, not an original sentence** (supplemented 2026-10-03).
Under the default permission tier
**official wording**: "your Muse will ask for permission before every write action and important read actions"
while the Connector page says the default state is **official wording**: "Muse will not take **many important actions**, like sending an email, without your approval" (note: many, not every).

The combined consequence is clear: **during background work reads keep running as usual, and any write must come back to the foreground and wait for approval**
— which matches the launch page's **official wording**: "comes back ... when it needs approval, like before it sends an email or makes a purchase".

**This is not an official sentence saying "background is read-only"; it is a mechanism conclusion derived from two permission clauses**,
and unlike Dot where read-only is stated outright, **do not quote them as the same sentence**.
axes.tools:
**The payment tool is the most distinctive item, and the official pages name the partner**:
**official wording**: "Muse can checkout with Link built by Stripe, and it is the first AI agent covered by Link's purchase protections", including free coverage for damaged or lost items,
price-drop protection, no-fee returns, and a return guarantee on eligible purchases.

The mechanism per the official pages: **official wording**: "Link's wallet for agents generates a one-time-use card so your real card details stay hidden".

Shop Pay **official wording**: "coming soon", plus 1Password support (also reusing logins you already have).

Browser capability is stated officially: **official wording**: "It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf".
axes.context:
**The memory mechanism is one of the official selling points**:
**official wording**: "Muse also remembers what matters to a person, so it can make suggestions unprompted and act on details that person only mentioned once"

The official examples are concrete (turning a recipe reel saved on Instagram into a shopping list,
re-sending an invitation after remembering a friend's dietary restrictions).

The Help Centre adds a sentence pinning down the **source** of memory:
**official wording**: "Muse is designed to remember context from your conversations, so you can refer back to things you've discussed before"

— i.e. conversations themselves are a first-class memory source, not only things you explicitly ask it to remember.

**The storage form is written officially as inspectable files, not a black box**:
**official wording**: "You can find out what Muse remembers about you at any time by asking directly, or by viewing files like your MEMORY.md".

The forget skill mechanism is also spelled out, with an **official hedge** attached:
**official wording**: "Forgetting works by asking Muse to look for information about a specific person, topic or matter in its memories and supporting files and remove it **to the best of its ability**"

**"To the best of its ability" is not a guarantee of complete erasure**, and this hedge deserves separate note.

**The deletion side also has official mechanisms**:
**official wording**: "You can delete any message you send to Muse, Side Chats with Muse, and files in your virtual machine"

Reset is supported, as is forgetting a specific topic (forget skill).

The official pages also warn about residue:
**official wording**: "Muse may still remember information it learned from what you deleted"

**This qualifier is worth noting: deletion does not erase what was already learned.**

**Residue has more than the deletion path (supplemented 2026-10-03)**. Disconnecting a Connector does not clear memory either.
**official wording**: "Information that Muse previously used to perform tasks with that Connector might still remain in Muse's memories and your conversation history".

**By contrast, reset is the hard boundary**:
**official wording**: "Resetting Muse permanently deletes all information, chat history, files and active tasks. **This cannot be undone.**"

⚠ **The context-window size is not published officially**; no official number has been seen.

One engineering detail is mentioned but not expanded: the VM **official wording**: "maintains backups to help protect your agent's history from data loss"

— **a backup mechanism exists, but neither page says how long backups are kept or how they interplay with deletion semantics.**
axes.permissions:
**This entry's most distinctive design: an independent Sentinel agent performs approvals.**

**official wording**: "A separate Sentinel agent runs on that same machine, kept apart from Muse at the system level. Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the Sentinel approves it, and it asks the person for permission when needed"

**i.e. approval is not judged by Muse itself but by another agent system-level isolated from it.**

This differs in implementation from Dot's "auto-review" (Dot never states whether its reviewer is independent).

The rest: asking before sensitive actions (sending email, purchases);
**official wording**: "Muse shows people a complete audit trail of everything it has done and plans to do"
(**the audit surface is broader than Dot's activity view — it includes "plans to do"**);

users choose apps and permission granularity themselves:
**official wording**: "for things like email, people choose what Muse can do, whether it reads their mail or can also send on their behalf";

**credential isolation**:
**official wording**: "Muse has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods. Any credentials a person shares with Muse go into secure storage",
and **official wording**: "Muse also cannot see passwords a person types into the browser themselves";

the Help Centre details the mechanism: three checks before using credentials (whether the service is the expected one,
whether you authorized it, whether you granted permission for this kind of action);

**training toggle**:
**official wording**: "People can also opt out of their interactions being used to train Meta's AI models"
(the Help Centre page adds: on by default, changeable anytime, and changes also apply to historical interactions;
when on, some identifying information such as names/emails/phones/SSNs is still removed and decoupled from the account);

**not shared with the ads system**. Both official Muse statements say conversations and VM data do not go to Meta's ads system.
The Help Centre page adds: the same holds even if other Meta products are linked in Accounts Center.

**⚠ The official pages themselves admit prompt injection is unsolved (supplemented 2026-10-03, first-hand wording)**:
**official wording** (four sentences quoted together): "Websites, emails, files and connected services can contain instructions intended to manipulate an AI agent." "This is sometimes called a prompt injection attack." "Muse uses multiple protections to help detect and resist these attempts." "These include model training, automated detection systems, and limits on the information and services Muse can access during a task."

**The key sentence**:
**official wording**: "Important permission and security checks operate separately from the AI model, meaning that they don't rely only on Muse recognizing that an instruction may be malicious."

— **the official pages admit "the model itself recognizing a malicious instruction" is not enough as a backstop**. This matches the Sentinel design motivation.

The official pages also state, as expected, **official wording**: "No automated system is perfect", and ask users to review activity themselves.

**⚠ Custom Connectors are a risk opening flagged by the official pages themselves (supplemented 2026-10-03)**:
users can have Muse build a connector on the spot, and the official pages immediately warn:
**official wording**: "Meta doesn't review custom connectors or how they use your information, so grant access with caution and review the provider's privacy policies."

— **this is an official admission of a review blind spot**, which must be counted when evaluating third-party integrations.

Permission convergence in the other direction also has official clauses:
**official wording**: "Many Connectors can also be set up so that Muse is only able to retrieve data, but not take actions (like sending a calendar invite)"

— **read-only connectors are an official de-escalation option.**

⚠ The Help Centre page contains one **not-yet-implemented promise**: Muse Confidential VM.
The official wording says **official wording**: "In the future / Later this year",
i.e. **the whole VM encrypted with a key only the user holds, unreadable even to Meta** — **currently unavailable**.

sections.与 Dot 的关键设计差异（两份同期档案，最值得对照的地方）:
| | OpenAI Dot | Meta Muse |
|---|---|---|
| Who approves | "auto-review", **independence of the reviewer not stated** | **independent Sentinel agent**, system-level isolation from Muse |
| How strict is approval | "certain sensitive tasks like changing passwords always require you personally" (translated) | "Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the Sentinel approves it" |
| Audit surface | activity view for progress | "complete audit trail of everything it has done **and plans to do**" |
| Credentials | uses stored passwords, not exposed to the model | Secure Credentials Store, and it cannot see passwords the user types |
| Entry points | ChatGPT / Slack / Teams / SMS | **WhatsApp** (like messaging another person) |
| Can it pay | not written on the launch page | **yes**, Stripe Link, with purchase protections |
| Training toggle | personal plans choose | Help Centre: "on by default, can be turned off, changes also apply to history" (translated) |
| Background autonomy permissions | **officially stated read-only** | **writes must return to the foreground for approval** (derived from the default tier's "every write action needs permission"; no official "background is read-only" sentence) |

**The last row deserves separate emphasis**: Dot's official pages **explicitly state** read-only; Muse's do **not** have that sentence.
After this supplemental verification, Muse yields a **mechanism-level conclusion** (the default permission tier requires permission for every write action,
so during background work writes must come back to the foreground and wait for approval),
**not an original "background is read-only" sentence**.
The two differ in strength; do not mix them when quoting — this boundary must still be held.
sections.Sentinel：一个独立的否决层:
```
A separate Sentinel agent runs on that same machine, kept apart from Muse
at the system level. Nothing Muse does reaches the internet unless the
Sentinel approves it, and it asks the person for permission when needed.
```

**The weight of this sentence lies in "kept apart at the system level"** —
not a prompt-level constraint ("please check compliance first"),
but another process/agent isolated at the system layer.

Implication: **Muse cannot grant itself a pass.**
This is a design of completely different strength from "relying on the model's own judgment about whether to ask".
sections.审计面比 Dot 更宽：含「打算做什么」:
```
Muse shows people a complete audit trail of everything it has done
and plans to do.
```

**Note `and plans to do`** —
what is audited is not only actions that happened but planned actions too.
This intervenes one step earlier than "reading logs after the fact" (the user can see what it plans to do before it acts).
sections.删除不等于抹掉（官方自己提醒的）:
```
You can delete any message you send to Muse, Side Chats with Muse,
and files in your virtual machine.
...
After you delete something from Muse, Muse may still remember information
it learned from what you deleted.
```

The official pages provide the forget skill (asking it to forget a topic/person/interaction),
and you can inspect `MEMORY.md` to see what it remembers.

**But the "may still remember after deletion" sentence is written by the official pages themselves** —
meaning **data deletion rights and model memory are two separate lines**; the former does not automatically cover the latter.
This must be examined separately in compliance assessments.
sections.Confidential VM：写下来了，但还没上线:
```
Later this year, Meta will introduce Muse Confidential VM, where the whole VM,
including a person's data and conversations with Muse, is encrypted with a key
only they hold, so not even Meta can access it.
```

**The official wording is Later this year / In the future — currently unavailable.**

If this were written into a selection conclusion as an existing feature, that would be treating a promise as fact.
This site marks it clearly: not implemented.
sections.支付：唯一一家官方点名支付合作方的:
```
Muse can checkout with Link built by Stripe, and it is the first AI agent
covered by Link's purchase protections: free coverage for damaged or lost items,
price drops, no-fee returns, and a return guarantee on eligible purchases.
Link's wallet for agents generates a one-time-use card so your real card details
stay hidden.
```

The mechanism is worth noting: **one-time-use card + checkout on the user's behalf**, so real card numbers stay hidden.
Shop Pay coming soon, plus 1Password support (also reusing existing logins).

**Compared with the other two**: neither Dot's nor Grok Bot's official launch pages mention the agent paying directly.
This is the only one of the three with an official payment-path statement.
sections.与数据面的具体边界:
The Help Centre page has a very concrete promise worth copying down:

```
For example, connecting your email allows Muse to search your email,
but it won't download your whole inbox (unless you tell it to).
```

**"Connecting email does not mean hauling away the whole inbox"** — this is the official least-privilege example.

Two more explicit promises:

- Conversations and VM data are not shared with Meta's ads system (**even when other Meta products are linked in Accounts Center**)
- Secure Credentials Store: credentials go into the vault, usable by Muse but invisible to it;
  and **it cannot see passwords the user types into the browser themselves**

**⚠️ One inconsistency in evidence method, recorded honestly**:
all three Help Centre pages are **full page bodies returned by the search interface**. Direct `WebFetch` of meta.com still fails from this machine.
The bodies are complete and quotable verbatim, but **were not rendered and captured locally** —
for formal external citation they should be re-verified once more.

**Confidence remains partial, but the reasons have changed twice**:
before the supplement it was because **"Help Centre direct capture timed out, only search summaries obtained"**;
after the supplement all three bodies are in, and what remains is **data the vendor simply has not published** —
context-window size, Sentinel decision criteria.
sections.三个值得单独记的官方自认风险:
The biggest gain from this supplemental verification is not what was filled in but **three limitations the official pages themselves admit**:

| Official wording | Implication |
|---|---|
| "No automated system is perfect" | the official pages do not promise the approval layer is free of misjudgment |
| "they don't rely only on Muse recognizing that an instruction may be malicious" | **official admission that the model judging alone is not enough as a backstop** |
| "Meta doesn't review custom connectors or how they use your information" | **official admission of a review blind spot for custom connectors** |

The second sentence corroborates the Sentinel design: **approval is placed outside the model precisely
because the official pages themselves consider "the model can recognize malicious instructions" unreliable.**
sections.残留记忆有四条路径，只有 reset 是硬边界:
Previously only "may still remember after deletion" was recorded. This round adds the second path — **disconnecting a Connector does not clear memory either**:

```
Information that Muse previously used to perform tasks with that Connector
might still remain in Muse's memories and your conversation history.
```

| Operation | What it clears | Official wording |
|---|---|---|
| Delete messages / Side Chats / VM files | that interaction and files | "may still remember information it learned from what you deleted" |
| forget skill | a specified person / topic / matter | "remove it **to the best of its ability**" (best effort, not a guarantee) |
| Disconnect a Connector | stops data exchange | "might still remain in Muse's memories" |
| **reset** | all information, chat history, files, active tasks | "**This cannot be undone.**" |

**This must be examined separately in data-deletion assessments**: in the official wording the first three all leave room;
only reset is deterministic.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs. The test protocol is at [protocols/coding/_protocol.md](../../../protocols/coding/_protocol.md).

**Suggested measurement**: a **same-topic contrast with OpenAI Dot** is the only meaningful design —
both launched the same period with close positioning. The differences concentrate in `permissions` (Sentinel vs auto-review)
and `context` (whether training is on by default).

Neither needs benchmarks, just reading settings pages + observing behavior,
but **measurement requires a paid subscription** (Muse currently launches in the US).
unknowns:
- Context-window size (no official numbers at all)
- Sentinel decision criteria and misjudgment handling
- Launch timing and form of the Confidential VM
- VM backup retention duration, and its interplay with deletion semantics
- Availability and feature differences outside the US
- Where the boundary of the free tier's "most of what people need" lies
related: **released the same period, must-read contrast** (different approval-layer designs)
released the same period, the third vendor
the local-CLI contrast (the machine is yours)
